title: Who Holds Copyright to Music Created by Band Members?
summary: In a U.S. band, copyright to music does not automatically belong to everyone who rehearses, performs or appears on the release. The starting point is authorship...
body_markdown:
In a U.S. band, copyright to music does not automatically belong to everyone who rehearses, performs or appears on the release. The starting point is authorship: who created the song and who created the recording. Contracts can then change ownership, licensing authority and payment rights.


**Band membership, songwriting credit and copyright ownership are different things.** A guitarist might own part of the composition but none of the master. A band company might own the master while two members retain the publishing. The answer depends on the contributions and the paperwork, not simply whose name appears on the artwork.


## Start by separating the song from the recording


A band recording usually involves two distinct copyrighted works. Each needs its own ownership analysis.


Work


What it protects


Ownership question


Musical composition


Original musical expression and any lyrics


Who wrote the song, and did they transfer any rights?


Sound recording, often called the master


The particular recorded performance and production


Who authored the recording, and what do the recording agreements establish?


Writing a song does not automatically give someone ownership of every recording of it. Likewise, performing on a recording does not automatically give someone a share of the underlying composition.


For a fuller explanation of the underlying work, see what[composition copyright gives songwriters ownership of](https://usethirdchair.com/blog/composition-copyright-what-songwriters-actually-own) . For band ownership disputes, the practical point is to maintain separate records for compositions and masters, even when the same people own both.


## Who holds copyright to music written by several members?


When members write together, the first question is whether they created a **joint work** . Under the[Copyright Act’s definition of a joint work](https://www.copyright.gov/title17/92chap1.html#101) , the authors must intend their contributions to merge into inseparable or interdependent parts of a unitary whole.


A lyricist and composer can therefore be joint authors of one song even though their contributions are different. They do not need to contribute the same number of words, notes or hours.


But participation alone is insufficient. Suggesting a mood, booking rehearsal space or saying “make the chorus louder” does not establish songwriting authorship. Courts examine the contribution, the parties’ intent and the applicable legal standard. The precise joint-authorship analysis can vary by jurisdiction.


A riff, bass line or instrumental passage may involve protectable musical expression, but **there is no automatic rule that every instrumental contribution earns a songwriting share** . A commonplace musical element may not qualify for protection by itself.


Keep dated demos, lyric drafts, session files and messages about collaboration. These can help explain what happened if the credits or ownership percentages are later challenged. They supplement a signed agreement rather than replace one.


## Does performing on the master create ownership?


The analysis of copyright to music changes when the dispute concerns the recording rather than the song. Sound recording authorship can involve performers, producers or both, depending on their creative contributions and the legal relationships involved.


Still, appearing in a session does not automatically establish an ownership percentage. Employment, work-made-for-hire rules, assignments and joint-authorship requirements may affect the result.


Consider three different roles: a member who writes the lyrics, a drummer who performs on the recording and a producer who shapes the recorded sound. Their potential rights arise from different contributions. Their contracts may also allocate those rights differently.


Paying for studio time does not, by itself, make the payer the copyright owner. Nor does possession of the session files prove ownership. Funding, authorship, control of the files and ownership of the copyright are separate questions.


For each master, identify the potential authors and review the agreements covering their contributions. Do not assume that composition splits also govern the recording.


## What happens when joint authors never agree on splits?


Under the usual U.S. default, joint authors hold equal undivided interests unless a valid agreement establishes a different allocation. Unequal creative effort does not necessarily produce unequal ownership.


That makes documenting copyright to music especially important when one member believes they wrote most of a song. Two joint authors may begin with equal interests even if one supplied considerably more material.


Joint ownership also affects licensing. Subject to contractual restrictions, a joint owner generally may grant a nonexclusive license to the jointly owned work without obtaining every other owner’s consent. That owner ordinarily must account to the others for their shares of licensing proceeds.


However, one owner cannot bind everyone to an exclusive license merely by signing alone. A co-owner also cannot transfer another owner’s interest.


These defaults can be commercially awkward. A band may want unanimous approval for political advertising, brand partnerships or particular sync uses. **That approval process should be written into an agreement** , not assumed from friendship or past practice.


A prospective licensee must still evaluate both composition and master permissions. Authority to license a song does not establish authority to license a particular recording of it.


## What should the band put in writing?


### Separate authorship, ownership and royalty percentages


A split sheet should identify the song, contributors and agreed percentages. It should also state what those percentages mean. Authorship credit, copyright ownership, publishing income and a contractual royalty participation are not interchangeable.


If the band wants equal economic treatment regardless of who writes each song, document that arrangement precisely. Equal payment does not necessarily require equal copyright ownership.


A practical agreement should address:


-


**Composition interests:** Who the writers are, who owns each interest and whether any publishing rights have been transferred.


-


**Master ownership:** Whether recordings belong to individuals, a band entity or a label.


-


**Licensing authority:** Who can approve uses and which decisions require additional consent.


-


**Income and expenses:** How receipts, administration fees and agreed recoupable costs affect distributions.


-


**Member departures:** What happens to existing rights, future income and unfinished recordings.


An agreement allocating copyright to music should also distinguish the rights in existing works from obligations covering future material. A broad promise to share “everything the band makes” invites disputes about solo songs, side projects and recordings completed after a breakup.


### Do not treat “work made for hire” as a shortcut


Under[17 U.S.C. §§ 201 and 204](https://www.copyright.gov/title17/92chap2.html) , ownership initially follows statutory authorship rules, while a transfer of copyright ownership generally requires a signed writing from the transferring owner or an authorized agent.


Work made for hire is a specific exception, not a label that automatically works whenever it appears on an invoice. It can apply to qualifying employee work created within the scope of employment. For specially commissioned work, it requires a signed agreement and a work within one of the statutory categories.


A standalone song or sound recording does not qualify merely because someone paid a freelancer to create it. Particular projects may raise additional questions about collective works or other statutory categories, so the actual facts matter.


When a label, producer or band company is supposed to receive copyright to music, counsel should evaluate whether an express assignment is needed rather than relying solely on work-made-for-hire language.


A producer’s royalty points also do not necessarily mean the producer owns part of the master. The agreement must distinguish ownership from a contractual right to receive money.


## A practical example: four members, different rights


Consider a hypothetical four-person band. Maya writes the lyrics and Leo writes the music. They intend to create one song and sign a composition split agreement allocating ownership equally between them.


The bassist and drummer perform on the recording but make no additional songwriting contributions. All relevant contributors then sign appropriate agreements assigning their master interests to the band’s LLC. Assume those agreements validly cover the rights involved.


The LLC’s operating agreement gives each member a 25% economic interest, subject to its distribution and departure provisions.


Asset or payment


Position in this example


Composition


Maya and Leo each own 50%


Master recording


The LLC owns it under the signed agreements


LLC distributions


Governed by the operating agreement, not the composition split


Songwriting income


Allocated under the composition ownership and applicable publishing agreements


Here, copyright to music is not divided into four equal personal shares simply because there are four members. Ownership of an LLC interest is also different from directly owning the LLC’s assets.


If the drummer leaves, the departure provisions determine what happens to that membership interest. Leaving does not retroactively turn the drummer into a songwriter or automatically undo the master assignments.


## What changes when a band member leaves?


A departure does not, by itself, cancel existing copyright ownership. If a former member owns an interest in a composition, they ordinarily retain it unless an enforceable agreement provides otherwise or they transfer it.


The continuing band may still perform the repertoire, subject to applicable licensing requirements. But creating new recordings, adapting songs, licensing existing masters and using a former member’s name or likeness can raise separate issues.


A departure agreement should distinguish old compositions, existing masters, unfinished sessions and future works. It should also address accounting access, unpaid royalties, approval rights and any buyout.


Buying someone’s instruments, paying their outstanding expenses or removing their distributor access does not automatically purchase their copyright to music. A buyout needs to identify the rights being acquired and satisfy the applicable transfer requirements.


For a catalog transaction, the buyer should review the original agreements and subsequent transfers. A departing member’s release may resolve one dispute without repairing an earlier missing assignment from a producer or session contributor.


## Keep ownership records separate from payment administration


### Build a usable chain of title


For each composition and master, maintain a record of the claimed owners, their percentages and the documents supporting that position. Include relevant split sheets, assignments, producer agreements, employment documents and amendments.


Match those records against publisher registrations, distributor information and royalty statements. Differences may reflect administrative errors, different percentage conventions or a genuine ownership conflict. Investigate before assuming that one database settles the issue.


Copyright registration is valuable, but it does not turn a nonowner into an owner or repair an invalid transfer. Follow a sound process for[music copyright registration and enforcement](https://usethirdchair.com/blog/copyright-office-basics-for-music-registration-and-enforcement) , using accurate authorship and claimant information.


When reviewing copyright to music for a release or acquisition, trace each claimed interest back to its author and through any subsequent transfers. A spreadsheet that lists “band: 100%” is not enough if nobody can produce the underlying agreements.


### Let accounting follow the legal allocation


Royalty administration should implement the agreed rights, not invent them. A payment instruction may tell an administrator where to send money without transferring the copyright itself.


A band’s accounting adviser might use[accounting workflow automation](https://www.just-use-ai.com/agence-automatisation-ia-cabinet-comptable) for invoice processing and payment reminders. Those administrative workflows should remain separate from decisions about authorship, ownership and licensing authority.


If the accountant receives conflicting payment instructions, resolve the conflict against the governing agreements. Do not rewrite ownership percentages merely to make a quarterly distribution easier.


## Frequently asked questions


**Does putting the band’s name on a release mean the band owns it?** No. A performing name or release credit does not establish copyright ownership. Determine who authored each work and whether rights were validly transferred to a band entity, label, publisher or another party.


**Can members agree to share songwriting income even if only one person writes?** Yes, members can negotiate an economic arrangement, subject to existing obligations. The agreement should distinguish income sharing from authorship credit and ownership. If it transfers copyright to music, use a properly drafted and signed instrument rather than relying on an informal payment practice.


**Does paying a producer mean the band owns everything the producer creates?** Not automatically. Payment alone is not an assignment. Review the producer agreement for ownership, licensing, royalty participation and any valid work-made-for-hire provisions. Confirm that it covers the actual project and contributors.


**Can a former member reclaim transferred rights after 35 years?** Some grants executed by authors may qualify for termination under Section 203, subject to detailed timing, notice and eligibility requirements. Works made for hire are excluded, and not every grant becomes terminable exactly 35 years after signing. Catalog owners should obtain specialist advice before treating older assignments as permanently settled.


## Resolve the rights before the next release


Create two ownership schedules: one for songs and one for masters. Compare them with the signed agreements, confirm who can approve licenses and document what happens when membership changes.


If the records conflict, have U.S. music counsel resolve the gaps before a release, sync deal or catalog sale. This article provides general U.S. information, not advice on a particular ownership dispute.
